content_units: Best Fit for Your Schedule
Because you work full time and can realistically study only on weekday evenings,   Plan 1 is more sustainable   and is likely the better default choice.
-   Plan 1 load:   6 hours/week over 8 weeks = about   1.2 hours per weekday
-   Plan 2 load:   10 hours/week over 5 weeks = about   2 hours per weekday
- For most full-time workers,   1–1.5 hours on weeknights is much easier to maintain   than 2+ focused hours every evening for 5 straight weeks
- Intro statistics usually benefits from   spaced practice  , not short-term cramming
Study Plan Comparison
Plan   Timeline   Weekly Load   Topics   Assessment Style   Sustainability for Weeknights   Likely Effectiveness
Plan 1   8 weeks   6 hrs/week   Probability; distributions; hypothesis testing; regression   Weekly quizzes     High       High   for retention and consistency
Plan 2   5 weeks   10 hrs/week   Probability; distributions; hypothesis testing; regression; ANOVA   2 full mock exams   Moderate to low   High only if you can sustain intensity
Best choice for your case   8 weeks   Lighter nightly load   Core exam foundations   Frequent feedback     Best match       Best balance
Why Plan 1 Likely Wins
-   Better fit for your real schedule
- Weekday-evening-only study makes consistency the main constraint.
- Plan 1 demands less cognitive energy each night.
-   More sustainable pacing
- Statistics concepts compound: probability supports distributions, which support inference and regression.
- An 8-week pace gives you more time to revisit weak areas.
-   Weekly quizzes are a strong learning tool
- Frequent low-stakes testing improves recall and reveals confusion earlier.
- This is especially useful for topics like p-values, confidence intervals, and regression interpretation.
-   Lower burnout risk
- Plan 2’s 10 hours/week is not impossible, but after full workdays it can become mentally expensive fast.
- A plan you complete consistently usually beats a stronger plan you struggle to maintain.
When Plan 2 Would Be Better
Plan 2 could be the better option if any of these are true:
- You already have some comfort with basic statistics
- The certification exam explicitly tests   ANOVA
- You perform best under short, intensive preparation
- You can reliably handle   2 focused hours every weekday evening
- You want more exam simulation through   full mock exams
The biggest advantage of Plan 2 is   exam readiness through mocks   and broader coverage. Its biggest drawback is   fatigue and reduced consistency  .
Practical Recommendation for Your Exam Date
Given your constraints, choose   Plan 1  , then add   2 mock exams near the end   if possible.
A strong version of your preparation would look like this:
-   Weeks 1–6:   Follow Plan 1 normally
-   Weeks 7–8:   Use quizzes plus mixed review
-   Final 1–2 weeks before the exam:   Add 1–2 full mock exams and targeted revision
-   If ANOVA is on the exam blueprint:   self-study that topic after regression or during final review
This gives you:
- manageable weekday workload,
- stronger long-term retention,
- lower burnout risk,
- and some of Plan 2’s exam-simulation benefits.
Decision for Sustainability vs Effectiveness
Most sustainable:   Plan 1
Most effective for your specific situation:   Plan 1, with added mock exams later
Higher-risk/high-intensity alternative:   Plan 2

If effectiveness means “best chance of sticking with the plan and actually learning the material well by exam day,”   Plan 1 is the stronger choice  . Plan 2 is only better if you know you can sustain heavy weeknight study and you specifically need ANOVA plus mock-heavy prep.
